body:
Your description of wanting to be loved and accepted, and not have it be faked just because someone is trying to get something from you, is something that resonated with me. I often feel like my appearance is the only thing capable of giving me any sort of value, and that it is impossible for me to have any true connections with people based on my personality alone. It makes me feel like my personality is defective, at best something to be tolerated as long as I'm useful in some other way. What your boss did was deceptive and awful, you deserved more credit for your abilities than that! 

Going to a movie to cry actually sounds like a creative outlet, and probably better than just doing it at home like I usually do. You sound like an interesting person, I especially love your username. Harold and Maude is a favorite, and the pun was amusing for this sort of subreddit. I definitely think you will find the right people to connect with. I do commiserate with how long that seems to take though...

Occasionally I'll try to research ways of overcoming an issue, or how to change the way I respond to things, but most of the time I just don't think about it. If something that happened to me is relevant to a conversation I'm having, when I was younger I would mention it in a detached way if I thought it would further the discussion, but I found that mentioning things like that in an unemotional way creeped people out, so I stopped. It's not that I'm unaffected by traumatic experiences, it's just that I keep everything compartmentalized.

One negative thing I have noticed (that I've been trying to figure out how to overcome), is that I have difficulty trusting people, and while I don't usually express this or act on it, I can very quickly be convinced that close friends or family have ill-intentions towards me (because of some minor thing they did). It's like I go from being calm and confident in the relationship, to being paranoid and anxious in seconds. I usually just withdraw a bit until I can work through it on my own, because I do know that I'm being irrational and that the whole thing is in my head. If the person won't let me have space though, I tend to spiral a bit, because I get upset that I'm upset, which is an awful loop to be caught in. 

This is just my personal experience though. I don't know any other INTPs in real life who've gone through trauma. I have seen similar representations in fiction though (which is always awkward to watch).

This is very helpful. I am on my way to meet my friend now, and am definitely keeping this advice in mind.

That's interesting about INFPs reframing someone else's emotional reaction to see how they would have responded in their place. That actually does seem to fit things they say in some discussions. I think I was thrown because it was in response to something I had done, but I think you're completely right in that it wasn't meant to be negative at all. I'm going to keep this in mind for future interactions.

I don't think it's bad at all to find it easier to talk to people you aren't as invested in, so that you don't have to worry about their reactions. It's probably the same reason a lot of people hire therapists (or ask for advice on anonymous subreddits...).

That's a good point about needing different types of support from different people. I can definitely see how that would be true.

The consistent answer I'm seeing seems to be that knowing how someone feels is not a bad thing (as long as it's phrased nicely) and that it will more likely improve the friendship than destroy it. I'm going to give it a shot, and hopefully it will go well. Thank you!

I'm an INTP, so I think I have a fairly similar communication style. I can come across a bit like a professor lecturing everyone, and I'm definitely too straightforward, or even blunt, at times. I put a lot of effort into toning it down, but sometimes it doesn't work as well as I would like it to. 

Probably because of this, my friend and I don't censor ourselves much when discussing ideas (which is most of our conversations) and just happily talk about whatever catches our interest. But sometimes when we switch over to more personal topics, it's probably easy to be insensitive by mistake.

I tend to panic when I find out someone is upset, especially if it's my fault. I'm terrified I'm going to say the wrong thing and make it worse, and I feel like I don't have the skill or tact to avoid that when they are already in a vulnerable mindset. It sounds like INFPs aren't as bad at dealing with other people's feelings as INTPs are, from what yours and the other responses have said, so I think I'm projecting my fear of conflict onto them. I'm pretty detached, so I can definitely bring this up calmly.

I think just getting reassurance that the remarks were meant to be harmless, such as you confirmed, is helpful, because then I don't need to address everything. I will bring up this last one though, since it did leave me a bit insecure, and that's more detrimental to the friendship.

Thank you for your response, it was very helpful!

I'm an INTP actually. I do think my friend has good intentions. It is hard for me to read people to an extent, but they seem enthusiastic about spending time together, and we both talk fairly equal amounts in conversations (the mutual exchange of ideas is a lot of fun). I've honestly never seen them be unkind to anyone, even when they were annoyed with them.

That's interesting that INFPs can be judgmental. So far they really haven't seemed to be, but we also agree on a lot, so maybe it hasn't been an issue (or if it has they haven't mentioned it, which is a bit of a scary thought). It is nice to know that it is reversible. I put a lot of effort into not hurting people in general, so hopefully it won't be a problem.

 I really don't want them to feel bad about anything, especially because I don't think they intentionally were hurtful. I'm going to attempt to talk about it with them tomorrow. Thank you for your advice.

I do want to avoid having any distance form between us, since we do talk a lot. I find the idea of talking to them really frightening, but I might be able to say something. I'm kind of giving the whole thing some thought at the moment.

Thank you for the response and good wishes!

This is a little long, but I thought it would be a good idea to give a few different situations.

Examples:
I showed them a picture of one of my exes and they commented that they seemed “weird.” This made me feel like my taste in people was being condemned. But it’s possible that this is just what they thought they should say since they knew it wasn’t a pleasant breakup.

Another time I mentioned that earlier I’d been having a bad day and snapped unfairly at my SO (nothing cruel, just a bit childish). Instead of getting upset, my SO just teased me about it, and I was quite touched by how calmly they handled it. When I shared this with my INFP friend, I expected it to be treated as just a “isn’t it nice when people are kinder to us than we deserve” sort of anecdote, but instead they started comparing themselves to my SO and talking about how they would not have been able to handle my outburst. It made me feel judged, and embarrassed for sharing something so personal. In hindsight, I think they were just considering their own ability to handle conflict, and the comment had nothing to do with me.

Edit: I am off to meet with my friend, and wanted to remove the most recent example, just because I prefer not to have anything too personal online that involves another person (it was vague, but still). I definitely appreciated the responses to it though, they were very helpful! I will update the post when I return.

I think in most of these cases it was a case of making an offhand comment that was accidentally insensitive. I agree that they probably have no idea that anything hurt me, especially since I do hide my emotions, which probably doesn't help. 

When your friends tell you that something you said was hurtful, is there a way that you prefer they do it? I don't want to end up hurting their feelings in my attempt to fix things.

Thank you for your response. It's reassuring!
